01.event: A bill of divorce signed by Androlinai of Neharde'a is found; Shmuel's father sends the question to Rabbi Yehuda Nesia
01.turn: Rabbi Yehuda Nesia replies that all of Neharde'a must be examined
01.outcome: Not stated; the instruction is cited as proof of a legal concern
01.summary: A bill of divorce was found in Neharde'a naming Androlinai. Shmuel's father sent the question to Rabbi Yehuda Nesia, who replied that all Neharde'a must be checked for another man of that name.
01.missing: Any action after the ruling; whether the examination happened or the woman remarried
01.reason: One event (a document found), then a question sent and a ruling, with nothing narrated afterward. Jeff ruled on 2026-10-25 that this shape is not a story, not even borderline, and here it is cited as evidence in a legal argument.

02.event: Ameimar permits Rav Huna bar Natan to marry a woman from Mehoza
02.outcome: Ameimar relies on his tradition from Rav Zevid
02.missing: Any event beyond a ruling and scholarly debate about it
02.reason: A ruling followed by an ordinary scholarly challenge and justification. There is no narrated action or change and no conflict beyond normal Talmudic dialogue.

03.event: While Rav Hamnuna studies before him, Ulla praises him but laments that he comes from Harpanya, a town of flawed lineage
03.turn: Rav Hamnuna is ashamed; Ulla asks where he pays his poll tax
03.outcome: Learning that he pays to Pum Nahara, Ulla declares him to be from Pum Nahara, clearing his lineage
03.summary: Rav Hamnuna was studying before Ulla, who praised him but regretted that he came from Harpanya, a town of flawed lineage. Rav Hamnuna was put to shame. Ulla asked where he paid his poll tax, and when he said Pum Nahara, Ulla declared him to be from Pum Nahara and so of sound lineage.
03.reason: There is a real conflict (a public slight on someone's lineage), an emotional reaction that counts as an event, and a change: the shame is resolved and his status cleared. That is more than ordinary scholarly back-and-forth.

04.event: Judges rule a case following Rabbi Tarfon
04.outcome: Rabbi Yohanan criticizes him for treating it like a Torah-law error
04.summary: Judges decided a case following Rabbi Tarfon. Reish Lakish overturned their ruling and restored the money, and Rabbi Yohanan criticized him for treating it as an error of Torah law.
04.missing: The facts of the case itself and any consequence of the criticism
04.reason: These are mostly rulings and a rebuke. But Reish Lakish's reversal is itself an act that changes something (it restores the money), which under the 65a limit keeps it at borderline rather than not.

05.event: Rabbi Zeira goes up to Eretz Yisrael and finds Rabbi Asi teaching a ruling
05.missing: Any event besides a journey that frames the transmission of a teaching
05.reason: A setting (arriving in Eretz Yisrael) frames a teaching. Under the Shabbat 147a ruling that is not enough for a story.

06.actor: Judges of Neharde'a; Rav Hana bar Bizna; Rav Nahman
06.event: Judges in Neharde'a rule, and Rav Hana bar Bizna collects, sustenance for daughters from movable property
06.turn: Rav Nahman orders them to reverse it and threatens to seize their houses
06.summary: In Neharde'a and in Pumbedita, judges ordered daughters supported from movable property, and Rav Hana bar Bizna actually collected the money. Rav Nahman ordered them to reverse their rulings or he would collect their own houses in compensation.
06.missing: Whether the reversal happened; the outcome
06.reason: Mainly rulings and an order. But there is an actual collection and a threat that shows conflict, so it is more than a case brought to a rabbi. The outcome is only implied, which leaves it borderline.

07.event: He makes his divorce conditional on not marrying by the New Moon of Adar
07.turn: When Adar comes, he claims he said Nisan
07.outcome: None; the Gemara analyzes the legal concern
07.summary: A man said his document would be a divorce if he did not marry by the New Moon of Adar. When Adar arrived he claimed he had said Nisan.
07.missing: Any action beyond the man's statements; any outcome
07.reason: Everything narrated is speech, with no real conflict and no change, and it is followed only by legal analysis.

08.actor: Rabbi Yehoshua; Rabbi Yohanan ben Nuri
08.event: Rabbi Yehoshua goes to study with Rabbi Yohanan ben Nuri and finds him sitting among trees
08.turn: He stretches a vine between trees and asks about sowing
08.outcome: Rabbi Yohanan ben Nuri answers: within ten cubits permitted, beyond prohibited
08.summary: Rabbi Yehoshua went to study under Rabbi Yohanan ben Nuri and found him among the trees. He stretched a vine between two trees and asked whether one may sow beyond it, and Rabbi Yohanan ben Nuri gave the ten-cubit rule.
08.missing: Any change or consequence beyond the answer
08.reason: A visit that frames a question and answer, cited as proof of a legal distinction. Stretching the vine only illustrates the question, so this matches the Shabbat 147a shape that Jeff ruled not a story.

09.actor: A man in Rabbi Ami's neighborhood; Rabbi Ami
09.event: Rabbi Ami publicly declares the man a mamzer
09.outcome: Rabbi Ami tells him the declaration has given him life
09.summary: Rabbi Ami declared a man in his neighborhood a mamzer. The man went about weeping, and Rabbi Ami consoled him that being publicly known had given him life.
09.reason: A real event (the public declaration) causes an emotional reaction, which counts as an event, and a response that reframes the man's fate. That is two actions, causality and change.

10.event: He rules in accordance with Rabbi Elazar
10.turn: He remembers that the ruling was doubtful
10.outcome: He says Rabbi Elazar may be relied on in exigent circumstances
10.summary: Rabbi once ruled following Rabbi Elazar. On remembering the dispute, he said Rabbi Elazar could be relied on in an emergency.
10.missing: The case itself and any consequence
10.reason: A ruling and a later remark, both speech, cited as legal evidence. Nothing happens to anyone and nothing changes.

11.event: The Ninth of Av falls on Shabbat and is postponed to Sunday
11.turn: They fast but do not complete it, because it is their family festival
11.summary: Rabbi Elazar ben Tzadok recalls that once, when the Ninth of Av fell on Shabbat and was postponed to Sunday, his family fasted but did not complete the fast because that day was their family festival.
11.missing: Any response or consequence; the report is cited as evidence of practice
11.reason: A report of what a family did, cited as evidence for a halakhic point, with no one responding and nothing following. That is the bare-report shape of R-C5.

12.actor: A brewer; the beer's owner; Rava
12.event: A brewer betroths a woman with beer sediment belonging to his employer
12.turn: The owner finds him and asks why he did not use the better sediment; the brewer brings the question to Rava
12.outcome: Rava rules the owner's remark is not consent, so the betrothal fails
12.summary: A brewer betrothed a woman with sediment from his employer's beer. The owner found him and asked why he had not used the better sediment. The brewer went to Rava, who ruled that such a remark counts as consent only for teruma, so the sediment was not his to give.
12.reason: Like Jeff's cow case: a man misappropriates property and uses it, the owner discovers it and responds, and a rabbi rules. There is more than one narrated action besides the ruling.

13.event: Someone asks the people of Judea about a mishna reading
13.missing: Any event beyond a question and answer
13.reason: A question and answer about textual readings, with no conflict and no event.

14.event: Rabbi Elazar misses the study hall and asks Rabbi Asi what was said
14.outcome: Rabbi Asi reports Rabbi Yohanan's ruling
14.missing: Any event beyond a setting framing a question and answer
14.reason: A setting followed by a question and answer about a ruling. Under the Shabbat 147a ruling that is not a story.

15.event: Rabbi falls ill; Rabbi Hiyya visits and finds him crying
15.turn: Rabbi Hiyya asks why he cries, citing signs of death
15.outcome: Rabbi says he weeps for the Torah and mitzvot he will lose
15.summary: When Rabbi fell ill, Rabbi Hiyya came in and found him weeping. He asked why, since dying in tears is a bad sign, and Rabbi answered that he was weeping for the Torah and mitzvot he could no longer fulfill.
15.missing: Any change or outcome after the exchange
15.reason: There are real events (the illness, the visit, the weeping, which counts as an event), but the passage is mainly dialogue and nothing changes, so it fits borderline shape 1.

16.actor: Abdan's daughters-in-law; Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi; a pair of Sages
16.event: Abdan's daughters-in-law rebel against their husbands
16.turn: Rabbi sends two Sages to examine them; told 'your husbands are coming', they retort 'let them be your husbands'
16.outcome: Their retort amounts to a refusal (Rabbi's ruling follows in the next segment)
16.summary: Abdan's daughters-in-law rebelled against their husbands, and Rabbi sent two Sages to examine them. When women told them their husbands were coming, they retorted, 'Let them be your husbands,' rejecting the marriages.
16.missing: Rabbi's ruling sits in the context segment, not the passage
16.reason: A real incident (a rebellion against marriages) draws a response (Sages sent) and a defiant act of refusal, with conflict and a change of status. That is more than a ruling on a case.

17.actor: Rabban Gamliel, Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya, Rabbi Yehoshua, Rabbi Akiva
17.event: The Sages' boat sets sail on Shabbat
17.turn: Two walk the whole boat; two stay within four cubits out of stringency
17.summary: The Sages were sailing from Pelandarsin when their boat put out to sea on Shabbat. Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya walked about the whole boat, while Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Akiva stayed within four cubits to be strict with themselves.
17.missing: Any consequence or change following the actions
17.reason: A real one-time incident, which the Gemara quotes from the Mishnah (counted as Talmudic under R-C1). But it has little causality or change, so it is borderline shape 3.

18.event: Rava asks Rav Nahman which tanna rejects retroactive designation
18.missing: Any event beyond a question and silence
18.reason: Ordinary scholarly questioning met with silence. That is standard rabbinic dialogue without real conflict or any event.

19.actor: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua
19.event: They conduct a halitza before five judges
19.reason: A bare report of what rabbis did, cited for its halakhic implication, with nothing following.

20.event: Rav Beruna teaches a ruling in Shmuel's name; Rabbi Elazar doubts it
20.turn: Rabbi Elazar has Rav Beruna show him Shmuel's lodging, goes to Shmuel, confirms the ruling, and challenges it
20.summary: Rav Beruna taught a ruling in Shmuel's name, and Rabbi Elazar doubted it. He had Rav Beruna show him where Shmuel lodged, went to him, confirmed that Shmuel had said it, and then challenged him with his own earlier statement. Shmuel fell silent.
20.missing: Whether Shmuel retracted (the Gemara asks in the next segment)
20.reason: It is mainly speech, but there are real actions (being shown the lodging, going to Shmuel) and a confrontation that ends in silence. That is borderline shape 1.
